blocks.text: VMs virtualize the whole machine, so every app carries a full operating system: large images, boot times in seconds to minutes, duplicated kernels and memory, and a guest OS to patch per VM. They also leave the application-packaging problem unsolved.

rows: GB-sized images; slow to copy and store
Seconds to minutes to start; slow scaling and CI
Memory and CPU overhead per VM; lower density
Patching, hardening and monitoring every VM's OS
The app inside is still installed by scripts or by hand, so drift continues inside VMs
Vagrant boxes are slow to rebuild and share

blocks.text: VM vs container at a glance
VMs aren't obsolete: when you need a different kernel, strong multi-tenant isolation or a full OS, they're still the right tool. Containers trade isolation for speed and density.

Q: "If VMs already provided isolation, why did containers take over application deployment?" A: "VMs carry a full OS per app: heavy images, slow boots, duplicated overhead and per-VM OS maintenance, and they don't standardize how the app itself is packaged. Containers package just the app and its userland, start in milliseconds, pack densely and give a single portable artifact."

items: VM = full OS per app: heavy and slow to start.
Containers trade isolation for density and speed.
VMs still win for kernel diversity and hard multi-tenancy.
